message: docs: refresh product, setup, and contributor guides

fix(security): Harden state persistence and authentication

Reject stale state writes, require shared production nonce storage, redact unexpected errors, and bound API and signer request streams.

Pin Anchor to 1.0.2 and add account-validation and stateful security regressions. Include the defensive audit report and local validation evidence.

Revert "fix(a11y): restore visible focus on form controls"

This reverts commit 1714b16, restoring f61ef9e. The browser's default
outline on inputs was removed on purpose: form controls have a designed
focus state instead. The composer's wrapper and the cap, vault and
model-key fields turn their border accent; the address-book and
allow-list fields turn it bright; the delete confirmation turns it red;
the onboarding funding chips outline the visible chip. 1714b16 stacked
the default outline on top of every one of those.

Each control keeps a visible focus indicator, so non-form controls keep
the global :focus-visible outline and form controls use their own.

fix(aegis): a preflight rejection records no signature

b5e0700 attached the pre-computed signature to every rejected
transfer, including ones the RPC refused at preflight. Those are never
broadcast. With preflight on (the default), every execution-time Aegis
refusal, such as a cap used up between preview and sign, left an
activity row whose Explorer link showed "transaction not found".

Return no signature on that path, as before b5e0700. A transaction
that landed and failed still carries its real signature, and the card
now reads "Not submitted; nothing moved." for a preflight refusal,
which is accurate.

fix(app): deleting the agent routes to onboarding again

55835be made a failed refresh keep the last snapshot as "stale"
whenever a policy was already loaded. After teardown the refresh
answers policy_not_found, but a policy was still loaded, so the app
stayed on the deleted policy's dashboard with a stale banner. Retry
repeated the same result. Before that commit the post-mutation refresh
surfaced the error, and the shell routed policy_not_found to vault
onboarding.

Treat policy_not_found as the answer it is: drop the loaded policy so
the existing no-policy path shows onboarding, and a later network blip
cannot bring the deleted policy back as a stale view.

docs(policy): the chat patch builder has no cross-cap rule

Its doc comment said it enforces maxPerTx <= dailyLimit "like on-chain
update_policy". Neither does, as the code 20 lines below and bcc2526
(which cites this path to justify dropping the dashboard's rule) both
say. The comment invited re-adding the rule that bcc2526 removed.

docs(deploy): save a contact before the maya example

9c49533 stopped seeding demo contacts, so the local run-through's
"try send 0.5 sol to maya" now answers "I do not have maya saved".
Say to save the contact first, with the chat command that does it.

chore: remove dead code and stale comments left by recent fixes

Each item is left over from a commit that changed its surroundings:

- CapRow's validate prop has had no callers since bcc2526 dropped the
  cross-cap rules it served.
- PraxisLogoFull was used only by the splash e41c171 deleted, and the
  logo comments still described that splash.
- 55835be made failed background polls mark the snapshot stale, but
  the poller comment still said they fail silently. The refresh comment
  also said "five" parallel reads beside the six it makes.
- 8b3e1bc's teardown guard checked for an unsupported token program
  after resolveMintInfo, which only answers for SPL Token and
  Token-2022. That branch could never run.
- resolveSelfOrContact's continuation became optional in 4f07eda. Every
  caller passes one, and omitting it would bring back the bug that
  commit fixed (a tapped option losing the amount and asset). It is now
  required.
- shared/src/provider.ts: fix a mis-indented phase line, and document
  client_error as the one code the server never sends.

refactor(app): show agent states by name instead of fail-open ternaries

8c240b1 mapped AgentState to text in three nested ternary chains (the
header pill, the sidebar and the session card). Each ended in a
bare "live" default. A state the chains did not name would have been
shown as "Agent live", the worst default a safety indicator can have.

The state names already are the display words. Render them directly,
using CSS capitalization on the session card. A new state now shows as
itself, and 23 lines of branching go away. Checked live and revoked in
the browser.

refactor(app): give both dialogs one modal primitive

d1ee246 moved ConfirmDialog and OwnKeyDialog to native <dialog> by
copying the same effect, class string and Escape/backdrop handling into
each. 4519b10 (overscroll containment) and 60e2a2b (focus return) then
had to make the same edit twice. The next modal fix would too.

Move that behaviour into a Modal in ui.tsx, beside the other shared
primitives. Both dialogs now render their content inside it. Behaviour
is unchanged: modal focus trap, Escape and backdrop dismissal (blocked
while busy), scroll lock, and focus returned to the opener. Checked in
the browser.

fix(proposals): resolve submissions that expire without landing

b5e0700 and 8f1cae1 persist a signed transfer as "submitted" and
reconcile it by signature. A lookup that finds nothing reads as
"pending". But a dropped transaction is the most common reason
confirmation is unknown on Solana, and it is never found. That card
stayed "Confirmation unknown, do not submit again" forever. compactState
never collected it, and every 12-second poll spent another
getTransaction on it.

Record the blockhash's lastValidBlockHeight with the signature at
submission. getTransactionOutcome reports "expired" when the chain is
past that height and the transaction is in no block. It reads the height
first, so a transaction that lands between the two reads is not
misclassified. Reconcile turns an expired submission into a blocked
card. It adds no activity row, since nothing happened on-chain. The
card's blocked footer now says only what is true of every signed block,
because an expired submission was not "rejected".

The architecture doc now covers the submitted/reconcile lifecycle,
which the earlier commits never described.

refactor(proposals): build transfer activity rows in one place

8f1cae1 copied the 12-field transfer activity row from signProposal
into reconcile, leaving three hand-built copies with the blocked
preview. A change to ActivityEntry would have to find all three.

Add logTransfer(proposal, result) beside the existing logSwapRejection
and route all three through it. Behaviour is unchanged.

fix(proposals): reconcile never overwrites a concurrent write

8f1cae1 persisted reconciled outcomes through commit(), whose conflict
path reloads and writes this snapshot over the newer document. That
last-write-wins is reserved for conversation data. Reconcile runs on
the 12-second get-proposals poll, so a conflicting write from another
instance could be reverted, including a proposal it had just claimed
or submitted. That proposal would read as pending and signable again.

Save with compare-and-swap instead. On a conflict, adopt the newer
state and leave the outcome for the next read, like the proposal claim
does.

fix(chat): a successful retry no longer leaves a stale draft behind

d987154 restored a failed message into the composer and also offered a
Retry button for it. The two did not know about each other: a
successful Retry left the old text in the input, one Enter away from
a duplicate proposal card.

The conversation now owns the draft, since several controls send
(composer, Retry, clarify and suggestion chips). A failure leaves the
draft untouched; a success clears it only when it is the text that
went out. The Composer becomes a controlled input.

fix(policy): stop cap edits claiming an unconfirmed change failed

a4b0c3b showed "Not saved. The policy was not changed." under a cap
editor whenever the owner action failed. Since f57148c/6b9346a an owner
transaction can fail as submitted_unknown: it reached Solana and may
have landed. The dashboard banner then said "do not retry" while the
editor said nothing changed.

Keep the editor open on failure and let the banner give the reason,
which is how the vault and other owner forms already behave.

fix(policy): unpausing an expired agent restores its session

4f8ee02 made "paused" outrank "expired" to match the on-chain check
order, which put the dashboard's "Unpause agent" button in front of a
paused+expired session. That button sent { paused: false } alone, and
update_policy rejects any write that carries an expiry in the past, so
the recovery action was guaranteed to fail on-chain.

Build both recovery patches with one helper, resumePatch, which also
restores the expiry when it has passed. The expired banner no longer
suggests rotating the key: rotate_agent never touches expiry.

fix(a11y): respect reduced motion on boot skeleton

The splash removal left a pulsing loader with no reduced-motion guard.
Gate it with motion-safe so it renders static instead.

fix(auth): keep 401 recovery working across session cycles

The provider captured the first session object, correct only because
it remounts on sign-out today. Read through a ref and reset the
once-per-session 401 flag on start so a future reuse still recovers.

fix(a11y): return focus after dialogs close

Both modals trapped focus without restoring it, dropping keyboard
focus to body on close. Remember the opener and focus it on cleanup.

fix(chat): disable retry while a send is in flight

Retry called onSend unconditionally while Composer and clarify
options respect the thinking flag. Guard it the same way so a
double-tap cannot queue a duplicate message.

fix(proposals): reconcile without holding the lock across RPC

get-proposals polls every 12s on the read path; awaiting Solana RPC
inside the per-wallet mutex blocked sends. Fetch outcomes first in
parallel, then reload inside the lock and apply only to proposals
still submitted under the same signature.

fix(api): submitted-unknown gets its own error code

PraxisSubmittedError carried code internal_error, so every RPC
confirm-timeout paged as an internal error and clients could only
regex the message. Add submitted_unknown across server, shared, SDK
and web client, and log it as expected rather than reporting.

fix(app): preserve server error detail in stale state

Background polls hardcoded an offline message and dropped the server
reason, so rate_limited/conflict detail never surfaced. Prefer the
server message and keep the original network error as cause.

fix(a11y): restore visible focus on form controls

Removing the default focus outline left only a subtle border-color
shift, which fails WCAG 2.4.7 on dark surfaces. Keep the accent
outline for inputs, textareas and selects.

fix(policy): drop invented cross-cap validation

On-chain update_policy and configure_token require each cap > 0 and
treat per-tx and daily as independent gates; the chat policy_change
path accepts the same states. The dashboard blocked maxPerTx >
dailyLimit, so two entry points diverged. Remove the UI-only rule and
share the live-price guard on the envelope switch button.

fix(policy): paused outranks expired in agent state

UI getAgentState returned expired for a paused+expired session while
on-chain agent_transfer and the server mirror check paused first.
Align the order so the pill matches the chain verdict.

fix(vault): show the vault's token balance, not just SOL

The demo faucet minted stock into the vault and buys spent it, but the
app only ever read the vault's SOL balance. PolicyView had no token
balance, so the dashboard and sidebar showed nothing for any SPL token.

- Server: refreshPolicy now reads the vault's associated token account
  for the envelope mint (SPL Token or Token-2022, program from the mint)
  and attaches it as vaultTokenBalance. A missing account is a real
  zero; an unreadable mint, malformed account or failed RPC leaves it
  unset (unknown, never zero) without failing the policy read.
- The teardown token check shares the same ATA read and decoder.
- UI: the balance, with its dollar value for priced stocks, shows on
  the Overview vault card, the Token transfers card and the sidebar.
  The mint symbol/decimals/price chain moved out of TokenEnvelopeCard
  into useTokenMeta so all three resolve it the same way.
- The faucet runs outside the provider, so it now triggers an immediate
  refresh (optional PraxisProvider.refresh) instead of waiting for the
  12-second poll.
- Mock mode seeds a USDC balance and debits it on send.

Verified: bun run check (549 tests + build); mock mode shows 1,250 USDC
in all three places and 1,200 after "send 50 usdc to maya".

Collapse the hackathon planning docs into three authoritative documents
and strip development-era references out of the code.

- README: rewritten against the codebase; now carries the devnet try-it
  flow, the on-chain proof, and the honest stock scope (a buy moves
  vault stock, it does not purchase it).
- ARCHITECTURE: absorbs the still-true PreStocks design (verified mint
  facts, one-envelope-per-wallet model, pricing, schedules, baskets,
  faucet); drops a stale gap and history narration.
- DEPLOY: absorbs signer deploy and the check-script catalogue; turns

- Delete STOCKLANA, STOCKLANA-ROADMAP, PRESTOCKS, PRESTOCKS-SPIKE,

- Fix stale facts: signer program id, a log key that is never emitted,
  PRAXIS_LOCAL_INTENT default, Token-2022 support in .env.example.
- Rewrite ~60 comments citing a deleted spec (§5/§9/§12) or roadmap
  IDs; regenerate the IDL (doc strings only). stockscheck now reads the
  pinned universe instead of a duplicate mint list.

Verified: bun run check (541 tests + build), stocksgate, moneyshots,
swapcheck, tokencheck, live stockscheck, aegis:test T1-T10, link check.

fix(build): self-host JetBrains Mono so Vercel builds stop failing

Google sometimes answers the JetBrains Mono stylesheet with
fonts.gstatic.com/l/font?kit=...&skey=... URLs. Turbopack carries each
font file as an internal import whose query must parse to exactly one
entry, and the "&" in that URL splits it, so the production build died
with "next/font/google queries have exactly one entry" on whichever
builder Google answered that way (Vercel iad1, not local).

Reproduced locally by mocking that response with
NEXT_FONT_GOOGLE_MOCKED_RESPONSES: the old layout fails with the same
12 errors on jetbrains_mono_79720a79.module.css, the new one builds.
JetBrains Mono is now next/font/local (latin, variable 400-500, 31 KB,
OFL license alongside); the other three fonts are unchanged.

docs: record the devnet program upgrade and its live proof

Aegis was upgraded on devnet (slot 503065818) with the token-window fix;
the on-chain bytes match the tested build. stocksbuycheck passes against
it on the app's OPENAI mirror, and a same-caps reconfigure kept today's
40 OPENAI spent. The submission now cites that run instead of the older
one on a different mirror, and the runbook records the upgrade and its
rollback.

fix(aegis): a cap change keeps today's token spend

configure_token reset token_spent_today on every call, even for the
same mint. Raising a stock's daily limit therefore granted a second full
allowance the same day ($400 spent of $500, raise to $600, and the agent
could move $600 more), and a signature that LOWERED the limit handed the
agent fresh headroom — the shape a compromised backend would propose.
update_policy already keeps the live window for SOL; the token envelope
now does too, and only a mint change (new asset, new units) starts a
fresh window.

LiteSVM T10 pins it and fails on the previous program. Account layout
and IDL are unchanged; the mock provider mirrors the new rule.

fix(policy): say how to fix a token-envelope refusal

"SPL token transfers are not configured" and "OPENAI is not the
policy's configured token mint" are what a new user sees when they buy
before picking an envelope, and neither said what to do. Both now name
the switch in Policy -> Token transfers.

docs(submission): judge-ready copy for the main track and PreStocks

Fills the links, adds a try-it-yourself path through the demo faucet,
maps the product onto the PreStocks bounty's own categories, and brings
the claims in line with what now ships: dollar buys and caps priced at
PreStocks, and a plainer statement that a buy moves stock out of the
guarded vault rather than purchasing it. The proof run is pinned to the
mirror mint it actually used.

feat(policy): show a stock envelope's caps in dollars too

Stock caps are token quantities on-chain, so the policy screen read
"0.0768 OPENAI" for what the owner set as $100. Each cap row now carries
its dollar value at the PreStocks price when the universe has one.

feat(stocks): devnet demo faucet so a judge's wallet can complete a buy

The real PreStocks mints are mainnet-only and the devnet mirrors were
minted only to the operator's wallet, so any other wallet could
configure an envelope and read a proposal but never land a buy. A
signed-in wallet can now mint $1,000 of the active mirror stock into its
own vault (Policy -> Token transfers), which also creates the vault's
and owner's token accounts.

Off unless PRAXIS_DEMO_FAUCET_KEYPAIR is set. Refuses non-mirror mints,
a mainnet cluster (genesis hash) and any mint the key is not the
authority of; 3 grants per wallet per day. Simulated on devnet against
the OPENAI and SPACEX mirrors: ATA creates and Token-2022 MintTo pass.

fix(tokens): prepare the owner's own token account for self-buys

A bare "buy $40 openai" settles into the owner's wallet, but neither
configuring the envelope nor "prepare accounts" ever created the owner's
own ATA — only the vault's and the address book's. Any wallet other than
the operator's (whose ATA the mirror-mint script created) had the
headline buy refused for a missing recipient account, with a remedy
that did not remedy it. Both owner transactions now include it.

fix(policy): a dollar cap sets the stock envelope, not 100 SOL

"Set my daily limit to $100" dropped the "$" and proposed a 100 SOL daily
cap: usually a raise, in a product whose buys are now priced in dollars.
A dollar cap now targets the active stock envelope at the PreStocks
price and is applied through configureToken; with no stock envelope it
clarifies instead. SOL caps without a "$" are unchanged.

Documents that configure_token restarts the token day counter even for
the same mint, a program change deferred past judging.

feat(stocks): read "buy $40 openai" as $40 of OPENAI

A "$" on a stock buy used to be a quantity: "buy $40 openai" moved 40
OPENAI, about $52k at today's PreStocks price, while "buy ai basket $60"
really meant dollars. Single and recurring buys now convert dollars at
the PreStocks tokenPrice with the basket's integer math, name the price
in the reply, and clarify when there is no price instead of falling back
to a quantity. Recurring buys fix their quantity at creation. Assets with
no price source (SOL, USDC) keep the quantity reading and say so.

Stock envelopes now default to $100 per tx / $500 a day at the PreStocks
price (the universe route carries it) instead of 200 / 500 tokens, so the
over-cap demo still blocks. Landing mockup, README, demo runbook, spec and
the CLI demo labels follow the new reading.

test(stocks): use a neutral name for the unknown-symbol filter case

The universe filter test used "TESSERA" as its unknown symbol. PreStocks
bounty exclusivity bars non-PreStocks pre-IPO tokens, so keep that name
out of the submission entirely.

feat(intent): parse with the owner's browser-held model key

Share one intent request module between server and browser; the browser
calls Gemini/Groq with a local-storage key and the server normalizes the
reading, rejects key fields at the edge, and falls back to the shared
parser with a notice. Review hardening: nested credential scan,
invalid-reading fallback, test type fix, key-button a11y label.

mobile: restore thread switching and creation

The sidebar owns the thread list and the "New thread" button, and is hidden
below 760px with nothing replacing it. On a phone you could neither start a
session nor return to one — you were stuck in whichever thread happened to be
most recent, and the mobile tab row only ever switched between Conversation,
Policy and Activity.

A picker showing the active thread plus a "+" now sits under that row, in the
conversation view only, so it costs nothing on the screens that do not need
it. Both live inside one mobile-only block so desktop renders no stray rule
where the row would have been.

Also dropped the sidebar's ⌘N hint. Nothing ever listened for it, and nothing
could: browsers reserve ⌘N, so the shortcut was unimplementable as advertised.

proposals expire in a week, not a day

Reconsidered against the promise recurring buys make. What goes stale on an
old card is the reading, not the action: the amount is fixed when the proposal
is built and Aegis enforces the envelope live at submit, so a week-old card
still moves exactly what it says. The fee, the simulated outcome, the
remaining daily envelope and the USD figure are the parts that drift.

So the bar is forgetting, not drift — and a day was strict enough to break the
feature. A weekly buy fired on Monday would have expired before Wednesday,
quietly turning "I set up a weekly buy" into "I must check in within a day or
miss it". A week keeps the schedule's promise and still refuses a preview from
last month.
aegis: name why the zero-amount guard sits ahead of the policy sequence

teardown and copy: stop describing state that no longer exists

Deleting an agent dropped the cached policy but kept the activity feed and
proposals, which describe a vault that is gone and an on-chain log that is
closed. Re-initializing lands on the same deterministic PDA with a counter
that restarts at zero, so a kept row would also collide with a new action's
identity. Teardown now forgets all three together.

The blocked-proposal banner asserted "the chain would reject it". That is
right for a cap or allow-list rejection — and the banner directly above it
already stamps those with the on-chain reason code — but wrong for the blocks
the backend makes before the chain is ever asked, such as an expired preview.
It now states what is true of every block and leaves why to the line that
knows.

ARCHITECTURE: record the one concurrency window left open. Owner policy edits
are read-modify-write against whole allow-list vectors and the program has no
compare-and-swap, so two edits built from the same read would clobber each
other. The window is one blockhash lifetime and the blast radius is a lost
allow-list entry; closing it properly needs a nonce on PolicyAccount, which
changes the account layout.

vault form: follow the rent invariant the program now enforces

Making the reserve explicit on-chain surfaced a UI that walked straight into
it. "Max" rounded the balance to four decimals, so on a vault holding
6.250000123 SOL it proposed 6.25 — a partial withdrawal leaving dust, which is
exactly the rent-paying state the runtime refuses. It now fills the exact
balance, because Max means all of it.

The form also warns before the signature rather than after the failure: a
partial withdrawal that would leave the vault under its reserve, or a first
deposit below it, is explained and the button disabled. Aegis reads the real
figure from the Rent sysvar and remains the authority; the shared constant
exists so a form can say so without costing a wallet round-trip and a fee.

docs: describe the system as it now behaves

ARCHITECTURE.md gained what the audit changed and what it made explicit: the
vault's rent reserve as an on-chain invariant, the schedule-fire claim
alongside the proposal claim, the proposal freshness contract, the owner-relay
draft binding, and the session as a spending credential rather than only an
identity. The trust-boundary section now separates "not trusted for
enforcement" from "not trusted as data" — indexer and quote-feed strings are
authored by third parties and are bounded at the seam — and records that
conversation history is never replayed to the model, which is what keeps
research from steering a later parse.

The gap list drops the signer rate limit (it exists now) and gains the two
honest ones left: the signer's audit lines need shipping somewhere durable,
and rate limits degrade to process-local when the shared store is down.

README: T1–T9, the parser chain as it actually is (two providers, then the
offline floor), and the proposal TTL in the flow it belongs to.

state + stocks: claim a schedule fire before emitting it; split baskets in integers

Schedule firing read the due set, built cards, then wrote last-write-wins. The
cron fans out across wallets and the same endpoint is reachable from a
signed-in session, so two callers could both see a schedule as due, both emit
a card, and the loser's write could revert the winner's advance — leaving it
due again next tick. The advance is now claimed with a compare-and-swap before
any proposal exists, so a fire is at-most-once; a crash between the claim and
the card misses a fire, which for money is the right direction to fail.

splitBasket computed (usd / price) * 10 ** decimals as a double. That silently
loses precision past 2^53, which a cheap token on a 9-decimal mint reaches at
about sixty dollars — and the result is not an estimate, it is the quantity
the proposal asks the owner to sign. The division runs in integer space now.

The provider factory documented that providers are never cached across
requests and then cached one for the no-wallet path. Nothing used it; the
branch is gone and the wallet is required, so the invariant in the comment is
the invariant in the code.

PrestocksEntry carried five fields nothing read — including a contract address
that is NOT the mint Praxis transfers (that comes from the configured
universe, which a devnet deploy remaps to mirrors). Taking it from a price
feed would have been a quote source deciding which token moves. Dropped, along
with the validation I had just written for it.

The per-period catch-up loop moved into schedules.ts as advancePast, where the
rest of the cadence arithmetic lives.

sdk 0.5.0: close the contract drift and make the session self-healing

The SDK ships its own copy of the wire types, and it had fallen behind the
server: ResearchData lost `name` and the whole `sources` trail, ResearchMetric
lost `exact` and `note`, TransferDetail lost `usdEstimate`, and the error union
had no `conflict` even though the API answers 409. A self-contained type
contract that silently omits fields is worse than no contract — callers see
`undefined` and conclude the server did not send it.

ask() hydrated cards one request per proposal. A basket reply carries eight,
so a caller doing nothing unusual could trip the read limit; it now uses the
batch endpoint the server already exposed, and that endpoint is on the public
surface as getProposals().

Sessions are deliberately short now, which means a long-running agent process
will outlive its cookie. Rather than have every caller write the same
catch-401-and-reconnect block — and have the ones who do not simply stop
working after a day — the client re-runs the handshake once on a 401 and
retries, when a signer is configured and the failing call is not itself an
auth call.

Minor: UnsignedOwnerTransaction gained the required `draft` token, which is
the breaking change behind the minor bump.

wallet auth: bind the session to the connected account; expire stale proposals

Account switching was invisible. The session cookie names one wallet for the
whole of its life, and nothing watched the extension: switch Phantom to
another account and the header showed B while every read, every proposal and
every agent transfer still ran against A's vault. Owner actions would have
failed at the fee-payer check — but an agent transfer needs no wallet
signature at all, so a click meant for B's money would have moved A's. A
different connected account, or an explicit disconnect, now ends the session.

The session is a spending credential, not just an identity: holding one is
enough to move value within the Aegis envelope, with no further wallet
signature. A seven-day default is a web-app habit rather than a decision about
that, so it is a day now, configurable, and shortening it binds sessions
already issued rather than only future ones.

Proposals had no expiry. Everything on the card — fee, simulated outcome,
remaining envelope, the USD figure on a stock buy — is a reading taken when it
was produced, and Aegis cannot tell whether the person authorized the card in
front of them or one from last month. Proposals now carry createdAt and the
signature gate refuses one older than a day, with a reason that says so. A
recurring buy fired this morning is still signable this evening; a preview
nobody read is not. This is a freshness contract, deliberately not a second
copy of the policy check — the chain remains the only enforcement.

rate limits and key custody: make the ceilings real

Rate limiting had three gaps that made it decorative where it mattered.

The client identity for unauthenticated limits read the leftmost
x-forwarded-for entry — a header the client sets. Behind a proxy that appends
rather than overwrites, every request arrives with a fresh identity and the
limit is opt-out. Platform-set headers now come first, with XFF as the last
resort and a note that a deployment relying on it must front the app with a
proxy that overwrites.

A shared-limiter outage returned "allowed" unconditionally. That is the right
instinct for availability and the wrong one for cost: the paths it guards
spend LLM calls and RPC fan-out. Redis failures now degrade to the
process-local limiter — weaker than shared state, not a blank cheque.

One message is not one unit of cost. /send now carries an hourly window
alongside the per-minute one, so a wallet cannot sit at the burst ceiling all
day.

Key custody: the signer service holds the one credential that can move value
out of every vault the deployment serves, and it had neither a ceiling nor a
record. It now refuses past a per-minute signature limit and logs every
outcome — refusals, limit hits, and each signature with its instruction,
policy PDA and amount. This process is the only component that sees every use
of the agent key, so it is the only place that can answer what was signed
while a token was leaked. The custody predicate returns that description
instead of a bare boolean, which is what makes the record possible.

prestocks: stop caching a failed fetch as "there are no prices"

The quote cache stored whatever the last attempt produced, including the
empty list a network blip produces, for the full 60s TTL. A basket buy is
all-or-clarify, so for that minute every basket in the product answered
"PreStocks quotes unavailable" — a provider hiccup presented as a product
limitation.

A successful response is still cached for 60s. A failed refresh now serves
the last good answer for up to five minutes instead, and only then gives up.
These are pre-IPO marks, the figure is on the card, and nothing moves until
the owner signs — a few-minute-old price is both more useful and more honest
than no price. An empty-but-valid body is still an answer and is cached as
one, so we do not hammer the feed for the same nothing.

Concurrent callers now share one in-flight request rather than each opening
their own.

trust boundaries: bound and normalize every string that comes from outside

Three sources feed strings straight into the product's own surfaces, and none
of them were treated as input.

A market indexer's `symbol` and `name` are chosen by whoever minted the token,
which is anyone. They reached the research card, the disambiguation chips and
the source trail unbounded and un-stripped. React escapes markup, so this was
never XSS — it is a 4KB "ticker" that destroys the card it lands on, and bidi
overrides and zero-width marks that let a value rewrite the line it sits in.
server/agent/untrusted.ts strips and bounds them at the seam. The indexer's
`address` is now validated as a real key there too, rather than being carried
as an identifier until something downstream happens to parse it.

PreStocks entries got the same treatment, plus an http(s) check on the URL the
research summary quotes into its own sentence, and NaN-safe numerics.
formatPrice echoed an unparsable provider string back as "$<whatever>"; it now
reports the metric as unavailable, which is what it is.

LLM output is input as well. normalizeIntent accepted any number of actions —
each one a simulation, RPC round-trips and a card to read — and fields of any
length. Capped at five actions (a clarify past that) and 256 characters.

Finally, the mint cache was keyed on the address alone while this process
talks to two clusters at once: the transfer RPC and the research RPC are
configured separately and routinely differ. A mainnet read could answer
"movable" for a mint absent from the cluster the transfer would run on. Keyed
by endpoint now.

aegis client: bind owner submits to the server's draft, fix audit-trail identity

Owner relay. The submit gate checked that the transaction's blockhash matched
a blockhash the same client supplied — a comparison that cannot fail. With
only the program allow-list left doing real work, a client could assemble its
own Aegis instructions and skip every precondition ownerActionInstructions
attaches to an action: the "your vault still holds tokens" refusal on close,
the movable-mint check on configure, the cap validation on updatePolicy. The
backend now fingerprints what it built, signs that with the session secret,
and refuses to relay anything else. Wallet-appended ComputeBudget priority
fees are excluded from the fingerprint, since wallets legitimately add them.

Audit trail. The on-chain log is a ring buffer, so an entry's array index
shifts every time a new action lands — and rows were keyed on it, minting a
new id for the same action on every refresh. Entries now carry the log's
monotonic `seq`. Separately, a confirmed transfer was recorded twice: once
locally at sign time (where the signature is) and once from the chain. The
two records of one transfer are now matched, with the durable on-chain row
keeping the local signature.

extractCustomErrorCode scanned program logs even when nothing had failed, so
a log line containing "Error Number: 6003" could report a landed transfer as
an Aegis rejection. It now returns early when there is no error.

PraxisConflictError documents itself as 409 and was answering 500.

aegis: make the vault's rent reserve an explicit on-chain invariant

The vault is a data-less system PDA, so the runtime rejects any transaction
that leaves it funded below the rent-exempt minimum. The program measured
every debit against lamports() instead, which meant three things were wrong:

- a partial withdrawal that left dust failed with InsufficientFundsForRent
  rather than a typed Aegis error;
- "the vault holds N" was read as "N is spendable" by agent_transfer, so the
  last ~0.0009 SOL was an unreachable cliff;
- a first fund_vault below the reserve failed for a reason nothing named.

vault.rs makes the reserve a first-class concept: the agent spends only above
it and can never deallocate the vault, while the owner may either leave it
rent-exempt or sweep it to zero. Zero-amount transfers, funds and withdrawals
are refused outright — they moved nothing, paid a fee, and wrote an audit-log
row saying an action happened.

Two new typed errors (ZeroAmount, VaultRentExemption), appended so existing
wire codes are unchanged, with the regenerated IDL and a test asserting the
TS error maps still cover every code the program declares. T9 in the
enforcement gate pins the new boundaries.

build(vercel): stop uploading 2.4GB of Rust build output on every deploy

Vercel honours only the root .gitignore, not nested ones. `aegis/target`
is ignored by `aegis/.gitignore` but Vercel never reads that file, so
every `vercel --prod` was uploading 2.4GB of Anchor build artifacts —
past the 2GB deployment limit, so the deploy could not have succeeded.

The Anchor program is built and deployed on-chain separately; the
Next.js build never reads that directory.

feat(intent): a second parser with its own quota, behind one transport

A single free tier is a single point of failure, and its failure mode is
invisible: the quota runs out, every request falls to the offline regex
parser, and the product keeps answering — worse. That has now happened
twice here for two different reasons (a retired model, then a 20/day
cap), which is enough to stop treating it as bad luck.

Adds an OpenAI-compatible transport and chains Gemini -> Groq -> offline.
Both score 17/17 on the intent sweep and return byte-identical parses on
live calls, so a hand-off costs latency and nothing else. Order is
PRAXIS_INTENT_PROVIDERS; a provider with no key is skipped.

One transport covers Groq, Cerebras, OpenRouter, Together and Mistral,
and it sends the tool schema untranslated — Gemini needs uppercased
types and no additionalProperties, and Groq 400s on exactly that
translation, so a test pins the untranslated shape.

Measured, because published limits did not survive contact:
  - Groq openai/gpt-oss-120b: 17/17, ~1.0s median. Its 30 RPM / 1000 RPD
    does not apply to a ~1.8K-token request — the 8K TPM / 200K TPD
    budgets bind first, giving ~4/min and ~100/day.
  - Groq's documented automatic prompt caching would exempt our constant
    ~96% prefix from those limits. It did not engage: cached_tokens was 0
    on every call, including four in a row seconds apart. Not budgeted
    for. `intent.llm_usage` now logs the spend so this is watchable.
  - gemini-flash-lite-latest: 15 RPM. Better burst than Groq, so it
    leads.
  - Cerebras is deliberately not wired up: its free tier answers 402
    payment_required on every model until a card is on file.

fix(intent): the default model allowed twenty free requests a day

Free-tier `gemini-flash-latest` is capped at 20 requests per day per
model (GenerateRequestsPerDayPerProjectPerModel-FreeTier = 20). Request
twenty-one is a 429, and a 429 lands in the same catch that a retired
model did: the silent fall back to the offline regex parser. Yesterday's
fix stopped the parser degrading on day one; this one stops it degrading
after twenty messages, which is the same bug wearing a different cause.

`gemini-flash-lite-latest` has real daily headroom, answers in ~0.9s
against ~8s, and scores 17/17 on a sweep of the intents this repo pins —
but only since the previous commit declared the nested tool schema. On
the unfixed schema it was 13/17, which is the honest reason not to
reach for a smaller model without measuring first.

Also records what "gemini-2.5-flash-lite" is: a real model name that
404s exactly like `gemini-2.5-flash`. The whole 2.5 family is retired
for keys issued now, so it is not the escape hatch it looks like.

GEMINI_MODEL still overrides. On a paid key with no daily cap, full
flash is the stronger parser and worth setting.

fix(intent): the recurring-buy cadence was prose, not schema

`cadence` was declared `{type: "object"}` with no properties, and the
shape it actually needs — type daily/weekly/monthly, weekday 0-6, day
1-31 — lived only in the description text. `assetIn` and `assetOut` had
no description at all. A large model infers all of that; a small one
does not, and measurably did not: on a 17-case sweep of the intents this
repo already pins, every recurring buy came back with an unusable
cadence and every swap dropped a required field. Four failures, all of
them a field the schema never declared.

Declaring the nested properties took that sweep from 13/17 to 17/17 on
the same model, with no prompt change. The prose stays where it helps
(which verb maps to which action) and stops standing in for a type.

fix(agent): a reply that fails is a sentence, not an internal error string

The catch-all around every reply was `error.message`, verbatim, so the
chat showed "intent field recipient must be a non-empty string" and
"Solana token supply lookup timed out after 8000ms". It also logged
nothing, so a failed reply left no trace for whoever had to explain it.

A parse that came back missing a field now asks for that field by name —
`readRequiredString` carries it in `details` — and a timeout names the
source without the milliseconds. Everything else is passed through
unchanged: an Aegis rejection or a mint the program cannot drive is
already written for the owner, and swapping those for "something went
wrong" would throw away the only useful part.

Adds an end-to-end suite over `send` covering the three transcripts that
started this: the ambiguous ticker asks and its answer round-trips as a
mint, the single match goes straight to the card, and a pasted mint
resolves with the stock universe enabled.

fix(research): an indexer outage costs the market rows, not the whole card

`fetchIndexerPairs` degraded a non-2xx to `[]` but let a timeout or a DNS
failure throw, and that throw escaped to the chat reply — so a four-second
hiccup at the indexer replaced the entire card, on-chain data included,
with "Token indexer lookup timed out after 4000ms". Every other read in
this file degrades; this one now does too, and the trail distinguishes an
outage (worth retrying) from a mint that genuinely has no market (never
will be).

Also tightens what the model is told about research: pass the ticker or
mint through exactly as written, strip the surrounding words, and never
invent or complete a mint address. Resolution is the server's job now,
and a hallucinated address would point the card at a real token nobody
asked about.

feat(research): the card shows its working

A read-only card whose whole pitch is "data, no advice" could not say
where a single number came from, and every gap in it looked identical —
one word, "unavailable" — whether the indexer had no pair for the mint,
the RPC refused the query, or the metric does not apply to that token at
all. Those are three different facts and only one is worth retrying.

Each card now carries the steps that produced it, collapsed behind
native `<details>` so the numbers stay the answer and the trail stays the
audit. Resolution leads, because "which of the four TRUMPs is this, and
how did we decide" is the first thing a reader needs to check. Failures
carry their cause: rate-limited, timed out, or a mint that is not on the
cluster the research RPC points at.

Endpoints are named by host only — a provider RPC carries its API key in
the query string, and this data is rendered to the client. There is a
test that holds that line.

Also documents the one gap operators can close: the public Solana RPC
rate-limits `getTokenLargestAccounts` into the ground, which is the only
reason "Top 10 concentration" reads unavailable on a default deploy.

fix(research): the card's numbers read as numbers, and "unavailable" says why

A supply printed as `87994397952881.85356` is a digit-counting exercise,
not a figure — nobody reads a magnitude off nineteen characters. Market
cap and volume had the same problem in the other direction, padded out to
`$295,929,398.00`, and the price formatter fixed four decimal places, so
every memecoin under a hundredth of a cent rendered as the identical
`$0.0000`.

Abbreviate for reading and keep the exact figure on hover: rounding is a
display choice, and dropping the precise value at the formatter would
make it a data loss. `Intl.NumberFormat` does the abbreviating, so the
suffixes and grouping follow the locale rather than a hand-rolled table.

Metrics also carry a note now, because "unavailable" on its own is a
shrug. "Top 10 concentration" is the one that reads unavailable on every
default deployment: `getTokenLargestAccounts` is the call the public
Solana RPC rate-limits hardest — 429 on essentially every request, while
`getTokenSupply` on the same mint succeeds — so the row now says what it
measures and why it is empty. Same for a mint with no indexer pair, and
for a supply that came from PreStocks rather than the chain.

The card also shows the project name beside the ticker: with four live
mints answering to TRUMP, "TRUMP" alone does not say which one it is.

feat(research): every Solana token resolves, and a shared ticker asks

Research answered from `config.tokens` — the four mints this deployment
can also *move*. Everything else hit `Unknown token "TRUMP". Try a mint
address instead.`, which is a demand rather than an answer: nobody has
the mint to hand, that is the thing they asked for. And the advice did
not even work, because `normalizeStockAlias` upper-cases every string it
does not recognise, so a pasted base58 mint was mangled before the
address check ever saw it.

Reading is not spending, so research now resolves against the indexer
instead: address, then the configured catalog, then a symbol search.

The catch is that a ticker is not an identifier here — four live mints
answer to TRUMP, six to BONK, eighteen to PEPE. Taking the deepest one
silently shows the wrong coin's numbers to somebody who will believe
them, so when the ticker is genuinely ambiguous the owner picks from a
liquidity-ranked list whose options round-trip as mints, and when it is
not, nothing is asked. A configured symbol still wins outright: "BONK"
in this deployment means the operator's BONK, never a clone.

fix(intent): research reads the coin, not the preposition in front of it

The offline parser took the word right after the research verb, allowing
exactly one preposition from a fixed list. Everything else became the
token, which is how three real transcripts came back as:

  "research about trump coin"     -> Unknown token "TRUMP"
  "research about 6p6xgHy…"       -> Unknown token "ABOUT"
  "research for this coin TRUMP…" -> Unknown token "THIS"

Skip filler words until a real one appears instead of enumerating the
prepositions people are allowed to use, and pull a pasted mint out of the
line first — an address beats a ticker when both are given, and a bare
address is the case a word matcher handles worst. A "$" prefix overrides
the filler list for a token genuinely named DATA or INFO.

fix(intent): the model was retired, so every message fell back to regexes

`gemini-2.5-flash` answers 404 for API keys issued now. Nothing broke
loudly, because `parseIntent` catches every Gemini failure and falls back
to the offline regex parser — so the product kept replying, with a parser
that reads "research about trump coin" as the token "ABOUT".

Default to the moving `gemini-flash-latest` alias so a retirement cannot
silently demote the product again, retry the transient 429/503 the free
tier hands out under load, and put the model name in the failure message:
"(404)" on its own does not tell an operator which name to change.

fix(intent): a "$" amount says which reading it took

`buy $40 openai` moves 40 OPENAI — about $8,700 at the current quote. The
sigil was matched by the amount regex and thrown away, so the product
accepted a dollar sign and silently meant something two hundred times
larger. Nothing was hidden (the real figure is the biggest text on the
card) but nobody should have to notice that for themselves on the screen
where they sign.

The call, and it is a call: the number stays a quantity. That is what the
program's caps, the stored schedules and `praxis:stocksbuycheck` already
mean by it, and reading it as dollars would quietly change what every
existing schedule buys and un-break the over-cap demo that proves the
thesis. Baskets keep their USD split — `buy ai basket $60` really is $60 —
and the README now says which is which instead of leaving both to
inference.

So the sigil is carried through the parse rather than dropped at the
regex, and the proposal reads: Reading "$40" as a quantity: 40 OPENAI, not
$40 worth of it. Two orders of magnitude is too far apart to leave to a
glance.

Also in this pass, from following the new path to the surfaces it reaches:

- The proposal card said "To: you" for a self destination, which on a
  labelled column reads like a value somebody forgot to fill in. It now
  says "Your wallet", off a `toSelf` flag derived from the ADDRESS rather
  than the phrasing — so it is right for a bare buy, for a schedule with
  no recipient, and for an owner who pasted their own address.
- Worse, the durable activity trail called it "Unlabeled recipient": the
  owner is never in their own address book, so the on-chain rows shrugged
  at the destination a bare buy produces every time. The audit log is the
  part of this product people are asked to trust; it does not get to be
  vague about its most common row.
- The delete dialog rendered the dashboard's shared action error, so it
  could open displaying whatever unrelated action failed last. It now
  shows only its own failure.
- Footer and SDK metadata pointed at `user-64bit/Praxis`, a handle this
  repo no longer uses; both now match the `public` remote.
- The walkthrough uses the documented `buy $40 openai` now that the card
  reads honestly for it.

fix(intent): "buy $40 openai" buys, instead of asking who for

The phrasing the README, the submission doc and the demo shot list all
lead with did not parse. It clarified, because the transfer shape needs a
`to|for <recipient>` tail — while `buy $50 spacex every monday`, the same
intent on a cadence, went straight through: `matchDca` leaves the
recipient undefined and `resolveSelfOrContact` defaults it to the owner's
own wallet. One sentence, two answers, depending on whether you said
"every monday".

A one-off buy now takes the same default. `transferBlock` routes through
`resolveSelfOrContact` instead of the address book directly, so both
paths agree on what "no recipient" means.

The part worth arguing about is how the executor knows. It is an explicit
`toSelf` flag, not an absent `recipient`, because those are different
sentences: "buy $40 openai" means *for me*, while "send 5 SOL to alex"
arriving without its recipient means something upstream lost a word. If
absence alone implied self, the second would quietly become a transfer to
yourself. So:

- Only buy verbs set it. A bare `sell` is a swap idea, not a transfer to
  yourself; a bare `send` still clarifies. Both are tested.
- The model path rejects a transfer that merely omits `recipient` — it
  has to say `toSelf`, and the prompt and tool schema say when it may.
- `transferBlock` refuses a transfer carrying neither, which the type
  still permits even though no producer emits it.

The default is safe in the first place because the destination is the
owner's own wallet: the agent moves your money to you, inside the same
Aegis envelope, and still refused if your recipient allow-list excludes
it.

The reply says which of the two happened rather than claiming an address
book hit for "you" — small wrongness on a proposal card is how people
learn to distrust the rest of it.

docs/PRESTOCKS.md said the union was unchanged and that this phrasing
resolved "via address book"; both are now accurate. The landing
walkthrough keeps `buy $40 openai for maya`: that scene is about
Token-2022, and a card reading "Send 40 OPENAI → you" invites a question
the scene is not there to answer.

fix(test): the suite no longer reads the developer's .env

`bun test` auto-loads `.env`, so the gate the CI workflow calls "the same
gate `bun run check` runs locally" was not the same gate at all: on a
machine configured for the devnet demo it failed four tests that pass in
CI's empty environment.

- `PRAXIS_STOCK_MINTS` (devnet mirrors) made `get-stock-universe` return
  mirror mints, so the route and universe suites saw the wrong mint and a
  duplicated OPENAI token.
- `CRON_SECRET` being set made "cron auth is unavailable when no secret is
  configured" assert the opposite of its name.

A test that passes or fails on whether the developer has configured a
cluster is not testing the code. `--env-file=/dev/null` gives the suite
the environment CI has; real process env still applies, so CI's own
`PRAXIS_LOCAL_INTENT` and the per-suite `process.env` fixtures are
unaffected.

fix(web): the landing lists what shipped, not what was planned in March

Three data files had drifted badly enough to misrepresent the product in
both directions.

Capabilities promised "scoped automation — Q2 2026" months after the
scheduler was firing, a keyboard-first command palette for "Q3 2026" that
has never been started, and gave cross-chain a card despite it being
explicitly out of scope. It said nothing about Token-2022, pre-IPO
stocks, recurring buys, wallet-signed owner actions, the on-chain
ActionLog, or the SDK — most of what the product now is. Rewritten as
nine things that exist; the roadmap belongs in "What's next".

Use cases advertised DCA and bridging as "not in v0.1" (one shipped, one
is not coming) and research as a 2026 item while it was already
answering. Every prompt on the page now parses in `server/agent/intent.ts`
— a prompt the parser refuses is worse on a marketing page than one
that's missing.

What's next opened with "recurring & scheduled action", which has been
running for weeks. It now starts where the code actually stops: swaps the
program can police, and making refusals as durable on-chain as approvals
are.

Why Praxis gains the token envelope in its list of guarantees, since the
program has enforced a second set of caps since the SPL path landed.

feat(web): a looping walkthrough replaces the one-shot demo and the mock-up

Two components each showed a slice of the product and neither showed it
for long. `CommandDemo` (the `#product` section) typed one blocked send
on page load and then sat frozen for the rest of the session — by the
time most people scrolled to it, the demo had already finished. Below it,
`AppPreview` was a static screenshot-in-HTML of a single SOL transfer,
carrying a ⌘K palette the app does not have.

`InsideTheApp` replaces both, in the slot the hero already pointed at. It
runs continuously through seven scenes and crosses all three surfaces of
the app: a send, an over-cap send the program refuses, a Token-2022
pre-IPO buy, a recurring buy, a policy change that needs the owner's
signature, the policy envelope, and the audit trail. That range is the
point — the old sections implied Praxis moves SOL and nothing else.

Fidelity rules it holds to:

- Every command parses in `server/agent/intent.ts`. A marketing page that
  demonstrates a phrasing the parser rejects is a support ticket with a
  countdown on it. (`buy $40 openai for maya`, not the bare
  `buy $40 openai` the docs use — see the README note in this PR.)
- Cards carry the Aegis verdict, in the wording `PolicyCheckBanner`
  uses, with a rejection styled as first-class as an approval.
- Signing swaps the card's buttons for its receipt, which is what the
  real proposal card does, rather than stacking a second card below.
- The window is a fixed height. Scenes differ by a couple of hundred
  pixels, and a product shot that grows and shrinks under the reader is
  the same jank this branch just removed from the app.
- Each thread opens with one turn of history, so the column is not empty
  while the next command is still being typed.

It pauses when scrolled out of view, and `prefers-reduced-motion` gets
the scenes at rest with the rail as the only way between them. The scene
entrance is transform-only: these surfaces are the content, and a fade
from opacity 0 leaves them blank for as long as a throttled tab takes to
start the animation.

`Sidebar`, `Thread` and `data/threads.ts` went with `AppPreview` — that
sidebar's thread list ("What's a Bonk?", "Slippage explainer") described
a product that was never built.

fix(web): landing copy that matches what the product does

A pass over claims that had drifted from the code:

- "Launch demo app" (hero and final CTA) — it is the app. Both now say
  "Launch app", and the footer's "Demo app" with them.
- "Aegis T1-T6 passing" in the footer and trust strip. The LiteSVM gate
  has covered T1–T8 since Token-2022 landed (f689062); T8 *is* the
  Token-2022 envelope.
- "Current scope: SOL / native transfers" in the trust strip, which the
  program outgrew in the same commit. Swaps had the value "v2", which
  named no version of anything; they are now "Not yet", with the reason.
- Twelve dead `href="#"` footer links — Documentation, Manifesto,
  Security, Press kit, About, Careers, Brand, Contact and four socials,
  none of which exist. The footer now links only things that resolve,
  including the Aegis program on the explorer: the program doing the
  enforcing should be one click from the claim.
- "In the live demo, the scoped agent key…" in How it works, which read
  as though enforcement were a demo affordance.

The Aegis program id moves to `@praxis/shared` as a base58 string so the
marketing page can name it without pulling in `@solana/web3.js`; the
server builds its `PublicKey` from the same constant.

fix(policy): a second confirmation before the agent is deleted

Typing DELETE and clicking the button closed the vault immediately. That
first step is weaker than it looks — the word to type is printed in the
placeholder directly above the field, so it can be completed by muscle
memory — and this is the one action in the product that ends the account.
It now arms the button; the button opens a dialog that states what
leaves, what comes back, and that revoke is the reversible version.

The modal chrome is extracted from RevokeDialog into a shared
ConfirmDialog, so both destructive actions get the same escape hatch as
the default focus, an error rendered next to the button that caused it,
and no dismissal mid-signature — the wallet prompt is already open at
that point and closing the dialog would orphan it (the revoke dialog
allowed exactly that on Escape).

Delete runs through the dashboard's shared action queue, so the dialog
stays open and busy for the whole wallet round-trip and closes only once
the delete lands; a failure is read in the dialog rather than in a banner
at the top of a scrolled page.

fix(policy): offer only the mints this cluster can actually move

Picking USDC, JUP or BONK under "No SPL token configured" walked the
owner through a wallet signature and then refused: "this mint is owned
by 11111111111111111111111111111111, which is neither SPL Token nor
Token-2022." The refusal was correct — the backend has checked mint
movability since 4f212ff — but the offer was not. The client carried the
list itself, three mainnet addresses, and showed them on whatever cluster
the backend pointed at. On devnet those addresses are plain System-owned
accounts.

Which mints exist is a fact about a cluster, so the server answers it.
`GET /api/praxis/get-token-catalog` resolves every configured non-stock
token against the transfer cluster and reports one of three states —
movable, wrong-program, missing — with the chain's decimals, which now
also beat the configured ones wherever they disagree. The pickers,
the "switch token" row and the allow-list quick-adds all read from it;
mints the cluster refuses are named with their reason rather than
silently dropped, so an operator pointed at the wrong cluster can see
that from the product. Mock mode keeps the static list: its provider is
the chain there.

`transferable` in the stock universe was the same class of claim — hard
-coded `true` — and is now the cluster's verdict too; a symbol it cannot
drive stays visible for research but is no longer selectable.

Both checks batch through one `getMultipleAccountsInfo` rather than N
serial reads, and a failed batch reads as "could not read", never as
"does not exist".

feat(aegis): Token-2022 support — stock buys can finally execute

Tokenized stocks are Token-2022. agent_transfer_spl hardcoded the classic
SPL Token program and a fixed 165-byte account length, so a PreStocks buy
was unexecutable — the headline feature of the submission could never
produce a landed transaction. This is the change that makes it real.

Program:
- Accept SPL Token or Token-2022. Both token accounts and the mint must
  belong to the SAME invoked program; mixing them is never legitimate.
- Token account length becomes `>= 165` (Token-2022 appends a type byte and
  TLV extensions to the classic base). Extended accounts must declare
  AccountType::Account, which is what stops a mint being passed where a
  token account belongs — the guard that keeps the relaxed length safe.
- The mint is now an account of the instruction, required to equal
  policy.token_mint, and the CPI is TransferChecked rather than the bare
  Transfer: the token program re-verifies mint and decimals on its side, so
  a mismatch fails there instead of moving a wrongly-scaled amount.
  Token-2022 also deprecates the unchecked variant.

Two deliberate non-changes, documented in the handler:
- A non-zero transfer fee debits the vault by `amount` and credits the
  recipient less. That is correct for a spending policy — the cap governs
  what leaves the vault.
- A mint with an active transfer hook needs accounts this instruction does
  not pass, so the CPI fails and everything reverts. A safe failure: no
  value moves and no untrusted hook program runs. Off-chain explains it.

Client: the token program is resolved per mint and threaded through every
ATA derivation. This mattered more than it looks — the program id is a SEED
of the associated-token address, so the old classic default didn't fail
loudly, it computed an address that would never hold the tokens.

T8 joins the LiteSVM gate: a Token-2022 transfer settles, the same per-tx
cap still bites, a mismatched mint account is rejected, and program
confusion, a mint-as-token-account, and an unknown token program all fail.
All 8 gates green against the real Token-2022 program.

fix(auth): shared single-use nonces, failing closed

Sign-in nonces lived in a per-process Map, so "single use" only held within
one instance. On serverless, an attacker who captured one valid (address,
nonce, signature) triple could replay it against a different instance for
the whole five-minute TTL and mint a second session. The check-then-set was
also racy: two simultaneous redemptions on the same instance both saw an
unused nonce.

Nonces are now claimed through a NonceStore with the same three backends the
rate limiter already selects between (memory, Upstash REST, native RESP), so
one Redis configuration serves both. The claim is a single atomic
`SET key 1 NX EX ttl`, which makes concurrent redemption a race exactly one
caller can win.

It fails CLOSED, unlike the rate limiter. A limiter outage must not take
down the API, so that one allows the request; a replay guard that degrades
to "allow" is not a replay guard, so this one refuses the sign-in and asks
the client to retry. The memory store likewise refuses at capacity rather
than evicting a live nonce, which would silently re-open replay.

The burn moved after signature verification, so a forged signature can no
longer consume someone else's pending challenge — previously the order made
that a cheap denial-of-service against a specific sign-in attempt.

fix(schedules): recurring buys fire on the day they promise

`advanceCadence` was `fromMs + 7 days` for weekly and `+ 30 days` for
monthly, ignoring the `weekday` / `day` the schedule actually stored. So
"buy $50 spacex every monday" created on a Wednesday fired every Wednesday
— while the confirmation message, the Activity list, and `describeCadence`
all said "every Monday". Monthly drifted backwards through the calendar by
a day or two each fire.

Cadence math is now real UTC calendar arithmetic: weekly walks to the next
occurrence of its weekday (a same-day match means next week, never the same
instant), monthly lands on its day-of-month and clamps to short months, so
a "31st" schedule fires on the 28th in February instead of spilling into
March. Time-of-day is inherited from the anchor, and UTC throughout means
no DST discontinuity.

`parseCadence` takes the clock as an argument instead of reading `Date.now()`
behind the caller's back — the module documents itself as pure, and the
anchoring behaviour for bare "weekly"/"monthly" is now testable.

Drops `cadencePeriodMs`, which only existed to express the wrong model.

fix(state): claim a proposal before signing it, with CAS-guarded writes

Two Fluid Compute instances serving the same wallet could each read the same
`pending` proposal and each submit an `agent_transfer`. The per-wallet mutex
that was supposed to prevent this is process-local, and persisting `signing`
before executing only helps a duplicate that lands on the *same* instance.
The Aegis caps bound the loss, but the user still sees two transfers leave
the vault. A regression test reproduces it: with the old blind claim, two
independently-loaded providers submit twice.

Durable state now carries a monotonic `rev` and every write is a
compare-and-swap against the revision it was read at (a single conditional
upsert in Postgres; a checked read-then-rename on the filesystem backend,
which only ever has one writer anyway). `signProposal` claims the proposal
through that CAS, so exactly one writer proceeds to submit; the loser
reloads, sees a non-pending proposal, and stops.

The conversational document keeps last-write-wins, but deliberately: reload
the newer revision and rewrite, with a warning logged, instead of silently

and the provider was compare-and-swapping against itself — every send logged

screen instead of setup.

`details`, both emitted in the JSON envelope. A missing policy is its own
`PraxisPolicyNotFoundError` with `code: "policy_not_found"` and the PDA in

field. Config (503) details stay in the operator log, matching the existing

fix(security): make shared-agent-key multi-tenancy an explicit prod decision

The backend holds one agent key and registers it as the agent authority on
every wallet's policy, so a single key compromise can drain every vault it
serves (each bounded by its own caps). That is fine for a single owner or
devnet, but the audit's top finding is that nothing stopped a production deploy
from silently serving many distinct wallets off that one shared key.

provider: in production, a wallet other than the single configured
AEGIS_OWNER_ADDRESS is refused under a shared in-process key unless remote
custody (PRAXIS_AGENT_SIGNER_URL) is configured or PRAXIS_ALLOW_SHARED_AGENT_KEY=1
explicitly accepts the model. Non-production and the single configured owner are
unaffected.

This converts a silent footgun into an explicit, acknowledged decision. True
per-owner key isolation (independent keys behind a remote signer / HSM) remains
the production end state; documented in .env.example.

- Remove the dead /subscribe route.

regardless of how many proposals exist. The persisted proposal set is already

the SDK.

fix(security): refuse non-Aegis instructions in owner-submit relay

The wallet-signed owner-action path built unsigned transactions server-side,
let the wallet sign them, and relayed them back via /owner/submit. Submit only
checked the fee payer and blockhash — not the instructions — so an authenticated
wallet could craft its own transaction (e.g. a raw SOL transfer) against a
backend-issued blockhash and have the backend relay it. Not privilege
escalation (the wallet is the sole signer), but it made the backend an open
relay for arbitrary wallet-signed transactions.

The owner-action builder only ever emits Aegis program instructions, so submit
now enforces an Aegis-only instruction allowlist on every transaction (always,
not just when a fee payer is expected), plus the existing fee-payer/blockhash
binding. Closes the relay surface without fragile instruction re-derivation.

transfer; happy path now uses a real builder-produced draft.

fix(provider): load state per request instead of serving a stale cached provider

getPraxisServerProvider cached one provider per wallet in module memory and
served every read/mutation from that provider's in-memory state, reading the
state repository only when the provider was first constructed. On serverless
(multiple Fluid Compute instances) a thread created and durably persisted by
one instance was invisible to another instance's cached provider, surfacing as
"unknown thread <id>" on the follow-up send.

- Build a fresh provider per request that loads the latest persisted state from
  the repository; the store is the single source of truth and every instance
  sees every write. Also avoids shared mutable state across concurrent requests.
- Route send's threadId through the idempotent newThread so a thread created in
  a prior request (possibly on another instance) is never rejected as unknown.

Contrast: Previously API mode inferred SPL activity labels from the current policy token mint. Now each allowed on-chain action records its own asset identity.

feat(aegis): prepare SPL token accounts

Why: The live SPL transfer path could be policy-correct but still fail because the vault or recipient associated token accounts had not been created. That made API-mode token sends fragile and hand-setup dependent.

What: Add idempotent associated-token-account builders, Aegis client setup helpers, a protected prepare-token-accounts route, provider support, a policy UI action, and a setup script. Configure-token now prepares the vault ATA when server-side owner signing is available.

fix(api): bound request abuse and dependency waits

Why: Authenticated API mode still needed bounded failure behavior. Without route limits or external call timeouts, a wallet or IP could spam expensive paths and LLM/indexer/RPC calls could leave user flows hanging.

What: Add in-memory per-scope rate limits for auth, reads, mutations, and agent sends. Add timeout helpers and apply them to Anthropic intent parsing, token indexer fetches, and read-only Solana research RPC calls.

Contrast: Previously requests were only payload-limited and external calls waited on provider defaults. Now common expensive paths fail quickly with explicit 429 or timeout errors.

Side Effects: Limits are process-local and should be paired with platform-level rate limiting in production. Timeout env vars can be tuned per deployment.

feat(server): persist wallet workspace state

Why: Wallet auth alone still left API-mode conversations, proposals, and rejected activity tied to process memory. A process restart could erase the off-chain audit surface that users need to understand agent behavior.

What: Add a compact file-backed state adapter keyed by wallet owner, persist threads, proposals, and activity on provider commits, and cap retained history to bounded sizes. Keep policy data out of the file and refresh it from Aegis as the source of truth.

Contrast: Previously each wallet-scoped provider started from a fresh welcome thread after restart. Now local/devnet API mode resumes the user workspace while on-chain policy remains authoritative.

Side Effects: Local API mode writes state under PRAXIS_STATE_DIR, defaulting to .praxis/state. This is a development storage adapter and should be replaced with managed database storage before production.

feat(auth): add wallet-scoped API sessions

Why: API mode needed a real owner boundary before any multi-user or production work could be meaningful. The public demo mutation token did not authenticate the wallet that owns the Aegis policy.

What: Add signed-message Solana wallet challenges, signed HTTP-only session cookies, an API auth gate, and wallet-keyed server providers. Protect all Praxis API reads and mutations behind the wallet session and keep owner keypair mutations limited to sessions that match the configured owner key.

Contrast: Previously API requests shared one process-global provider and mutations trusted a public header token. Now the signed-in wallet scopes policy, threads, proposals, and activity, while mock mode remains standalone.

Side Effects: API mode now requires a browser wallet sign-in before loading app data. Server-side owner policy actions still require PRAXIS_OWNER_KEYPAIR to match the signed-in wallet until wallet-signed admin transactions are implemented.

fix(api): bound demo inputs and clean UI accessibility

fix(app): surface mutation failures and require fresh rotation keys

What: Keep API mutation failures local to chat, proposal, and policy controls; add inline error surfaces; require `PRAXIS_NEXT_AGENT_KEYPAIR` for rotation; reject same-key rotation; and make the mock rotate into a distinct demo key.

Contrast: Previously most mutation promises were swallowed and remote mutations could replace the whole app with an API error screen; rotate-agent also fell back to the current agent key when no next key was configured.

docs(product): align claims with Aegis demo

Why: The landing page and README described wallet signing, beta access, and executable Jupiter swaps more strongly than the repository actually supports.

What: Rewrite setup docs around mock and API modes, document the demo mutation gate, point CTAs to the app, and revise product copy to emphasize native SOL transfers, policy rejections, revoke, research, and swap stubs.

Contrast: Previously the product surface mixed current capabilities with future roadmap items, which made the demo look broader but less trustworthy.

Side Effects: The marketing page is more conservative; it now frames swaps and owner-signed wallet administration as future work instead of shipped behavior.

fix(aegis): enforce policy admin invariants

Why: The policy owner path could put Aegis into unusable states with zero limits, expired sessions, or a default agent authority, and transaction confirmation used a fresh blockhash instead of the signed one.

What: Validate limits, expiry, and agent authority on initialize/update/rotate, add the matching LiteSVM gate case, expose a top-level Aegis test script, and confirm Solana transactions with the original signed blockhash window.

Contrast: Previously only transfer enforcement was strongly tested; admin mutations trusted caller input and client confirmations could be tied to the wrong validity window.

Side Effects: Existing demo policies with zero limits or expired update requests now fail with typed Aegis errors; the checked-in IDL includes the new operational error.

fix(app): make API mode fail visibly

Why: Remote mode was initialized from mock seed data, so missing backend configuration could look like a working live policy surface.

What: Add provider connection state, render explicit API loading/error screens, remove mock seeding from the remote provider, and route mutation failures into visible provider errors.

Contrast: Previously API mode silently showed fake demo state until refresh completed or failed, and failed mutations could surface as unhandled promises.

Side Effects: API mode now fails closed when the live backend cannot load; standalone walkthroughs should use the mock provider intentionally.

fix(api): gate Praxis mutations

Why: API mode could expose server-side signer and policy-admin routes to any caller, which made accidental public deployments unsafe even for a demo.

What: Require a same-origin request plus an explicit demo mutation token for all POST routes, wrap request parsing in the shared API error handler, and tighten primitive validation for policy patches and allow-list kinds.

Contrast: Previously mutation handlers accepted unauthenticated browser or curl requests and some parsing errors escaped the normalized JSON error path.

Side Effects: API-mode demos must set matching `PRAXIS_DEMO_MUTATION_TOKEN` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_PRAXIS_DEMO_MUTATION_TOKEN`; mock mode is unchanged.

feat(server): complete M2 Aegis executor contract

Why: Milestone 2 needs the backend and shared package to consume the generated Aegis contract and preserve the no-guess address-book rule before routing agent actions.

What: Add the generated Aegis IDL and type helper under `/shared`, derive server discriminators from that IDL, improve fuzzy address resolution so it asks for clarification, and format executor previews in SOL policy terms.

Contrast: Previously the TS client carried parallel discriminator bytes and fuzzy recipient input fell through to a missing-contact response; now the client is tied to the generated contract and fuzzy matches are never auto-selected.

Side Effects: No on-chain account layout, frontend component, or `praxis.html` changes. Runtime imports now depend on `/shared` exporting the generated IDL JSON.

test(aegis): tighten enforcement gate coverage

Why: The M1 gate is the proof point for Aegis, so the suite should match the prompt boundary wording exactly instead of relying on broader under-limit and rollover cases.

What: Assert the daily-limit `-1`, exact, and `+1` lamport cases, and add an explicit `>24h` rollover path while preserving the exact `>=86400` boundary check.

Contrast: Previously T1 used a coarser under-limit daily spend and T2 only demonstrated the exact rollover boundary; now both the literal prompt scenario and the off-by-one guard are covered.

Side Effects: This only changes the LiteSVM test harness output and does not alter on-chain program behavior, account layout, or frontend code.

feat(aegis): add policy vault enforcement

Why: Move delegated agent safety from backend promises into an on-chain policy vault that physically limits what the session key can spend.

What: Add the root Anchor workspace pinned to Anchor 1.0.1 and Solana 3.1.15 with `PolicyAccount`, a SOL vault PDA, owner-only policy/vault controls, revoke/rotate, action logging, events, and `agent_transfer` enforcement for signer, pause/expiry, per-tx cap, daily rollover, daily cap, and recipient allow-list checks.
